Key Characteristics & Etiology: Blunt lower chest or left hypochondrial trauma (RTAs, assaults, direct kick).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Laceration of splenic capsule/parenchyma causing hemoperitoneum and phrenic nerve irritation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe LUQ pain, peritonitis, Kehr's sign (left shoulder pain), Ballance's sign. Red Flag: Hypovolemic shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: FAST ultrasound / Contrast CT. Management: ATLS resuscitation, emergency splenectomy, post-splenectomy vaccines.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Temporal bone fracture with laceration of middle meningeal artery.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Rapid arterial bleeding expanding between skull inner table and dura mater, raising ICP.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Transient LOC -> Lucid Interval -> Rapid neurological deterioration, headache, ipsilateral dilated pupil.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Non-contrast CT Head (biconvex/lenticular hyperdense mass). Management: Mannitol/Hypertonic saline, emergency craniotomy/burr hole.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Tearing of bridging veins between cortex and dural sinuses (elderly, alcoholics).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Venous bleeding accumulating slowly between dura and arachnoid mater.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Gradual headache, cognitive decline, focal neurological deficits over days to weeks.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Non-contrast CT Head (crescentic hyperdense/hypodense extra-axial mass). Management: Surgical burr hole drainage.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: High-energy blunt head trauma fracturing anterior or middle cranial fossa floor.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Dural tear creating direct communication between subarachnoid space and paranasal sinuses/ear canal.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Battle's sign (mastoid ecchymosis), Raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis), CSF rhinorrhea, CSF otorrhea.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: High-resolution Non-contrast CT Head. Management: Conservative head elevation, avoid NG tube, observe for meningitis.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Penetrating or blunt chest injury creating a one-way valve pleural defect.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Air enters pleural cavity on inspiration but cannot exit, causing lung collapse and mediastinal shift.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe dyspnea, tracheal deviation to opposite side, hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical diagnosis (do NOT delay for X-ray). Management: Immediate needle thoracocentesis (2nd ICS MCL / 5th ICS AAL) -> Chest tube.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Penetrating chest trauma lacerating pericardium or coronary vessels.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Blood accumulates in pericardial sac, restricting ventricular diastolic filling and cardiac output.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Beck's Triad: Hypotension, Muffled heart sounds, Elevated Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: FAST ultrasound (Pericardial fluid). Management: Emergency pericardiocentesis / Subxiphoid pericardial window / Thoracotomy.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: High-velocity blunt impact fracturing >= 3 contiguous ribs in >= 2 places.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Segment of chest wall becomes detached, moving paradoxically inward during inspiration.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Paradoxical chest wall motion, severe chest pain, dyspnea. Red Flag: Underlying severe pulmonary contusion.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Chest X-ray / CT Thorax. Management: Analgesia (epidural/intercostal block), oxygenation, mechanical ventilation if hypoxic.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Direct flame, hot liquid scalds, or contact thermal injury.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Coagulative necrosis of epidermis/dermis; capillary leak causes massive third-space fluid shift.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Blisters, erythema, loss of sensation in full-thickness; hypovolemic burn shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: TBSA evaluation (Rule of Nines / Lund-Browder). Management: Parkland formula (4 mL x kg x %TBSA Ringer's Lactate), IV analgesia.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Thermal and toxic chemical exposure from smoke in enclosed space fires.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Upper airway thermal edema + lower airway chemical tracheobronchitis and ARDS.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Soot around nostrils/oropharynx, singed nasal hairs, hoarseness, stridor, disorientation.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy, ABG (Carboxyhemoglobin). Management: 100% humidified O2, early elective endotracheal intubation.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Full-thickness circumferential eschar over anterior and lateral chest wall.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Rigid unyielding eschar acts as a tourniquet, restricting chest wall expansion and ventilation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe respiratory distress, shallow rapid breathing, high peak airway pressures on ventilator.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical examination. Management: Emergency chest escharotomy (transverse subclavicular and xiphisternal incisions connected laterally).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Severe polytrauma with lethal triad: Hypothermia, Acidosis, and Coagulopathy.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Abbreviated initial surgery prioritizes rapid control of bleeding and contamination, avoiding prolonged reconstruction.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Hypothermia (<35°C), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2), non-mechanical microvascular bleeding.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Lethal triad laboratory markers. Management: Phase I (Emergency laparotomy) -> Phase II (ICU resuscitation) -> Phase III (Definitive repair).
